stories.headline: Tamil Nadu on rain alert? Bay of Bengal system may intensify into Cyclone Arnab by October 26
stories.title: Tamil Nadu on rain alert? Bay of Bengal system may intensify into Cyclone Arnab by October 26
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: A new low-pressure area over the southeast Bay of Bengal could intensify into Cyclone Arnab by October 26, raising concerns over heavier rainfall in Tamil Nadu amid the active northeast monsoon.

Chennai: With the northeast monsoon already bringing heavy rain to Tamil Nadu, a fresh weather system over the southeast Bay of Bengal could worsen the state's rainfall woes and intensify into Cyclone Arnab by October 26.
A weather department update reported by Dinamalar identified a new low-pressure area over the southeast Bay of Bengal.
The system is expected to strengthen into a depression the following day, before potentially developing into a cyclone on October 26.
If it develops into a cyclone, the system is expected to be named Arnab.
Bangladesh proposed the name under the regional cyclone-naming system.
The emerging system comes as Tamil Nadu is already witnessing heavy rain amid an increasingly active northeast monsoon.
Its further development could intensify rainfall across several districts, raising concerns about additional pressure on the state's civic infrastructure.
Heavier downpours can strain urban drainage systems, disrupt road movement and complicate routine civic operations, particularly in areas already experiencing persistent monsoon rain.
However, the available weather update does not specify which districts could receive the heaviest rainfall or provide estimates of expected precipitation.
There is also no confirmed information in the update on the system's projected landfall location, anticipated wind speeds or likely trajectory.
The precise extent of its impact on Tamil Nadu therefore remains uncertain.

stories.headline: IMD Update: Possible Bay of Bengal Cyclone by Monday; AP, Odisha on Alert
stories.title: IMD Update: Possible Bay of Bengal Cyclone by Monday; AP, Odisha on Alert
stories.summary: A parent low-pressure area is expected to move west-north-westwards over Bay, intensifying into a deep depression by Sunday and a cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay by Monday morning
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Bay of Bengal is brewing a potentially powerful cyclone, with the India Meteorological Department (IMD) hinting at its formation by Monday as a parent low-pressure area emerged over the south-east and adjoining east-central Bay on Friday morning.
The system is expected to move west-north-westwards, intensify into a deep depression by Sunday, and become a cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay by Monday morning.
It is then forecast to strengthen further and head towards the north Andhra Pradesh and adjoining south Odisha coasts over the next two days.
Global models suggest it could reach at least severe cyclonic storm intensity.
Meanwhile, another low-pressure area is holding sway over the south-east Arabian Sea, off the south Kerala coast, setting the stage for an intriguing interaction between the two systems.
The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts had suggested last week that the Arabian Sea low and the developing Bay cyclone could feed off each other, helping both systems strengthen.
Under that scenario, the Bay system would approach the Andhra Pradesh-Odisha coast, while its Arabian Sea counterpart would move northwards along the Kerala-Karnataka coast towards Goa.
The IMD, however, envisages a different twist to the tale.

Strong south-westerly flows feeding the systems could steer the Arabian Sea low back across the South Peninsula towards the south-west Bay, close to south Tamil Nadu and north Sri Lanka, from where it originated.
Thereafter, it could merge with the developing cyclone over the larger Bay.
Such a convergence could give the north-east monsoon another powerful burst next week, keeping the Southern Peninsula firmly in the rain belt even as the Bay system gathers strength.
Another rain-bearing system is in the forecast as Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal recover impressively from a distressing south-west monsoon season between June and September.

stories.headline: Karnataka Policy Panel member proposes NewWay National Security Framework for 2027–2037
stories.title: Karnataka Policy Panel member proposes NewWay National Security Framework for 2027–2037
stories.summary: The proposal calls for integrating defence preparedness, internal security, economic stability, technological advancement, critical infrastructure protection, essential-resource security, disaster management and constitutional governance under a coordinated national resilience approach.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'national security' in title weight 70
article_sentences: The proposal calls for integrating defence preparedness, internal security, economic stability, technological advancement, critical infrastructure protection, essential-resource security, disaster management and constitutional governance under a coordinated national resilience approach.

Bengaluru: Member of the Karnataka State Policy and Planning Commission, S. Mohanadass Hegde, on Friday proposed a NewWay National Security and Strategic Resilience Framework for 2027–2037, urging the Union government to examine a comprehensive approach to strengthening the country's long-term security and preparedness.

According to the proposal, national security extends beyond conventional defence and includes interconnected risks arising from disruptions to energy supplies, digital infrastructure, international supply chains, public health systems, water resources and essential public services.

The framework identifies 16 components for policy consideration, covering defence and military security, internal security, cybersecurity, critical infrastructure, economic and financial security, energy, water and food security, public health, climate and disaster preparedness, strategic technology, space and maritime security, supply chains, information resilience, institutional governance, citizen preparedness and international diplomacy.

It recommends examining these areas through common principles, including coordination among institutions, risk-based prioritisation, human oversight, constitutional safeguards, Centre-state cooperation, measurable outcomes and financial accountability.

A key recommendation is a periodic National Strategic Risk Assessment to identify vulnerabilities, existing safeguards, capability gaps and possible mitigation measures across security, economic, technological and environmental sectors.
The proposal emphasises protecting classified, sensitive and personal information, with public reporting restricted to information suitable for disclosure.

The framework also suggests examining secure digital coordination systems and the use of artificial intelligence and predictive analytics for risk forecasting, infrastructure mapping and early warnings.
However, it states that consequential security, legal and administrative decisions should remain with authorised human officials.

It proposes building on existing institutions, including CERT-In, the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC) and disaster-management authorities, within their respective mandates, rather than duplicating responsibilities or creating unnecessary parallel structures.
The proposed roadmap envisages four phases.
The 2027–2028 period would focus on reviewing existing policies and identifying coordination gaps.

stories.title: Rajasthan High Court Admits Appeal Against SC/ST Ward Reservation Over Allegedly Fake Population Data, But Refuses To Stay Election Process
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Rajasthan High Court has admitted an appeal challenging the reservation of wards in Gram Panchayat Majhiwala for persons belonging to Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs), allegedly based on incorrect population data, but refused to stay the ongoing Panchayat election process.
The Division Bench of Chief Justice Sanjay K. Agrawal and Justice Baljinder Singh Sandhu declined...

The Division Bench of Chief Justice Sanjay K. Agrawal and Justice Baljinder Singh Sandhu declined to interfere with the election process, observing that the State Election Commission had published the election programme for Rajasthan's Panchayat elections on October 3, 2026, thereby setting the process in motion.
Article 243-O of the Constitution restricts judicial interference in electoral matters relating to Panchayats, with the objective of preventing disruption of the election process.
The petitioner challenged the reservation of wards in Gram Panchayat Majhiwala for SC/ST candidates, alleging that the population figures used for the reservation were incorrect.
He contended that there were only 14 voters belonging to the Scheduled category in the Gram Panchayat and, therefore, the reservation ought not to have been made.
The petitioner also challenged the notification concerning the reservation of the Sarpanch post for Panchayat Samiti Majhiwala.
A Single Judge dismissed the writ petition as not maintainable in view of Article 243-O, since the election programme had already been published.
The petitioner subsequently filed a special appeal before the Division Bench.

The petitioner argued that the election programme was issued on October 3, 2026, but the election notification contemplated under Rule 23 of the Rajasthan Panchayat Raj Election Rules, 1994, had not yet been issued.
Therefore, he contended, the constitutional bar under Article 243-O was not attracted.

stories.headline: When practical short-term action meets long-term strategic thinking
stories.title: When practical short-term action meets long-term strategic thinking
stories.summary: In a quarter century of public service, Prime Minister Narendra Modi has demonstrated an extraordinary ability to link practical short-term action with long-term strategic thinking. In that spirit, my review of Indian economic performance over the same period has two goals. The first is to identify intrinsic strengths of the economy that have revealed themselves in our long-term performance. The second is to assess how these might guide policy in the critical period that lies ahead.Growing EconomyTo me, a striking fact is that the Indian economy has grown at an average rate of 6 percent between the start of this century until Covid hit in 2020. These data (based on national sources) are the basis of published detailed long-term analysis by, among others, the World Bank. They are the best we have for a fast changing, growing economy where, of necessity, reality outpaces measurement.There are other successes of recent Indian experience, including low inflation, reduction in absolute poverty (measured in terms of personal consumption) and declining consumption inequality, but here my focus is on growth, as ultimately, it is sustained economic growth that makes these other achievements affordable.Also Read: When households became shareholders: The quiet story of India's balance sheetSustained economic growth over a long horizon is not unprecedented in global post-war economic experience. This was the case in some countries now classified as high-income (Japan, South Korea) and those still on their way, most notably China. Even so, India’s growth achievement remains significant.Measured economic growth of any economy (such as the recent print of 7.8 percent annual growth for the first quarter of FY27) is determined by the interaction between aggregate supply and aggregate demand. Particularly in the richer economies and increasingly in India, short-term fluctuations in aggregate demand drive measured growth. Such demand fluctuations occur along an arc defined by the supply side of the economy.Sustained growth of aggregate supply reflects the steady accumulation of the most basic inputs (the ‘factors of production’: Capital and labour but also environmental inputs such as land and water). Labour includes demographic and behavioural factors (such as the willingness or ability of women to seek employment), and, crucially, improved health and better education (human capital).Classical economic theory proposes a ‘law of diminishing returns’, where the application of each marginal unit of these factors generates a lower return. In a democracy, this principle is reinforced by electoral compulsions. Accumulation of either physical or human capital implies deferred consumption. If undertaken by government, this implies taxation or increased debt. For all these reasons, the most important but also most elusive factor in sustaining long-term growth is innovation in the way these factors are used, commonly called technical progress, or, more geekily, growth in ‘total factor productivity’, TFP growth in short.In an ideal world we would have authoritative studies of the sources of Indian growth divided between factor accumulation (what the economist Paul Krugman has called ‘perspiration’) and TFP growth (‘inspiration’). Despite heroic efforts by the Reserve Bank of India to put out consistent data to support such analysis, I have not been able to come up with many recent studies of economy-wide growth in India’s TFP. China is an economy that has continued to devote vast resources to investment but is paying the price both in low shares of consumption and diminishing returns to capital formation.Also Read: Can the Indian economy grow fast even as prices rise?The US is a country whose extraordinarily steady GDP growth of 2 percent per year for almost a century has been much studied, in an environment where the underlying data have, at least until recently, been above reproach. Indeed, the formalisation of growth theory and the focus on TFP came out of an attempt to explain the US growth record despite indifferent investment rates. My reading of that literature is that the steadiness reflects the institutional flexibility of a vastly more affluent country than India today. And it is noteworthy that that this long-run steadiness has been maintained through war and peace, boom and slump.Flexible GovernanceWhat conclusions do I draw from India’s past record, based upon the US experience on the one hand, and the Chinese experience on the other? And what guidance does India’s past provide for our choices in future?On the first, the 25-year record suggests that the economic management framework (political and administrative) India had achieved by 2000—50 years after becoming a republic (and nine years after cautious embrace of global markets)—has proved resilient to shocks, including the one we are currently experiencing. My own recent experience in government suggests that there is deep underlying political consensus on a mixed economy and on social protection which may inhibit radical change.On the second question I would offer a series of observations. First, 50 years is probably a better horizon for both planning and assessing social and economic transformation. We are today half-way toward the prime minister’s aspiration of a modern, empowered society in 2047, something that crucially depends on sustained economic growth.Second, it would be a fatal mistake to assume that, despite the past record, steady 6 percent growth is assured. It is not, and we are where we are only because our style of governance has proven to be flexible. We are still not affluent enough to worry about the middle-income trap, but we are fortunate to have a large pool of current and prospective workers so that labour availability will not be a constraining factor for the coming decade.My final thought, derived from the discussion earlier, is that our policy focus should be less on sectors and more on factors of production: Labour, land and capital. We have not succeeded in top-down industrial policy in the past. There is little reason to think we will do better in the future. We are a more balanced economy than China and every bit as entrepreneurial as the US. We should take comfort from the fruits of past liberalisation and trust the genius of our population to make the best of the new opportunities that technology offers.

stories.headline: Architect of ambition: What 25 years of Modi means for business
stories.title: Architect of ambition: What 25 years of Modi means for business
stories.summary: When I founded ReNew in 2011, the hardest conversations I had weren’t with engineers, policymakers or bankers. They were with investors.The question was always a version of: Will the India of today still be there 20 years from now?Renewable energy is a business of long horizons. A project built today must generate reliable returns for 25 years. Investors were not evaluating a power plant; they were evaluating a country. They wanted to know whether policies would endure, infrastructure would materialise, institutions would strengthen, and whether India could maintain direction over decades rather than months.What they were looking for was constancy. Predictability.I have met many political leaders who follow where markets lead. It is rare to meet one who decides where a country should go and then patiently builds the road.Looking back over Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s 25 years in public life, first as Gujarat chief minister and then as prime minister, that quality stands out the most. Not simply ambition, but constancy of ambition. An ability to see something before it becomes obvious, pursue it patiently, and remain committed until a nation begins to believe in it too.Also Read: How India has learnt to build the impossiblePursuit of executionI have had the opportunity to meet Prime Minister Modi on several occasions. That instinct, to see beyond the next election, pursue relentlessly and govern for the next generation, is perhaps the most valuable thing a leader can offer an entrepreneur like me. Businesses can adapt to almost any direction. What we struggle with is uncertainty.That sense of certainty and pursuit of execution that Prime Minister Modi has brought has changed the feel of India. As I travel across the country to our project sites, I find it in thousands of everyday scenes. Village after village remains lit long after sunset. Roads reach places that once felt disconnected from opportunity. Border settlements that seemed remote are now linked by highways, telecommunications and reliable power.Towns like Sanand, Dholera, Hosur, Thrissur and Sri City, which barely registered on the economic map 25 years ago, are today attracting global capital, producing for international markets and creating opportunities for millions. Small towns that we once simply drove through are now crowded with warehouses, apartment blocks, hospitals, hotels, logistics parks and bustling marketplaces.Women who once organised daily life around the absence of toilets, reliable electricity or clean cooking fuel increasingly enjoy a degree of dignity and convenience. Small businesses accept digital payments from customers. Young creators from places far from India’s traditional centres of opportunity now participate in a national economy connected by roads, phones and digital networks.The biggest change is not any individual programme. It is that prosperity feels more widely distributed.One senses movement. One senses confidence. Above all, one senses that millions more Indians now expect their children to live better lives than they did. Of course, none of this emerged from a vacuum.Connective tissueIndia’s progress did not begin in 2014. It was built upon institutions, reforms and capabilities accumulated over decades. But the defining feature of Prime Minister Modi’s era has been the game-changing acceleration, scale and execution brought to those foundations.In earlier years, the transformation often happened incrementally and slowly. A road here. A bank account there. A digital platform. A tax reform. An electricity connection. A logistics corridor. Individually, each reform seemed limited.Under Prime Minister Modi’s leadership, they were pursued together. Only because someone at the top insisted they be pursued together did they form the connective tissue that allowed the economy to function with greater coherence. They created conditions for private capital to be deployed, not merely promised.They were accompanied by stronger public institutions and public sector enterprises, not as relics of an earlier era but as instruments of national capability. Whether securing oil supplies, acquiring critical minerals, supporting defence manufacturing, kickstarting clean energy markets or helping create new industrial ecosystems, they increasingly acted with the confidence of a country determined not merely to participate in global supply chains, but to shape them.Brick by brick, India has been building. Faster in some areas, slower in the others, but with a visible spine connecting the effort. That confidence has also been tested.Over the last decade, India has navigated a pandemic, global supply chain disruptions, energy price shocks, conflicts in Ukraine and West Asia, and a more fragmented geopolitical landscape. opening: When I founded ReNew in 2011, the hardest conversations.
I had weren’t with engineers, policymakers or bankers.
body: They were with investors.
The question was always a version of: Will the India of today still be there 20 years from now?
Renewable energy is a business of long horizons.
A project built today must generate reliable returns for 25 years.
Investors were not evaluating a power plant; they were evaluating a country.
They wanted to know whether policies would endure, infrastructure would materialise, institutions would strengthen, and whether India could maintain direction over decades rather than months.
What they were looking for was constancy.
Predictability.
I have met many political leaders who follow where markets lead.
It is rare to meet one who decides where a country should go and then patiently builds the road.
Looking back over Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s 25 years in public life, first as Gujarat chief minister and then as prime minister, that quality stands out the most.
Not simply ambition, but constancy of ambition.
An ability to see something before it becomes obvious, pursue it patiently, and remain committed until a nation begins to believe in it too.
Pursuit of execution.
I have had the opportunity to meet Prime Minister Modi on several occasions.
That instinct, to see beyond the next election, pursue relentlessly and govern for the next generation, is perhaps the most valuable thing a leader can offer an entrepreneur like me.
Businesses can adapt to almost any direction.
What we struggle with is uncertainty.
That sense of certainty and pursuit of execution that Prime Minister Modi has brought has changed the feel of India.
As I travel across the country to our project sites, I find it in thousands of everyday scenes.
Village after village remains lit long after sunset.
Roads reach places that once felt disconnected from opportunity.
Border settlements that seemed remote are now linked by highways, telecommunications and reliable power.

Towns like Sanand, Dholera, Hosur, Thrissur and Sri City, which barely registered on the economic map 25 years ago, are today attracting global capital, producing for international markets and creating opportunities for millions.
Small towns that we once simply drove through are now crowded with warehouses, apartment blocks, hospitals, hotels, logistics parks and bustling marketplaces.
Women who once organised daily life around the absence of toilets, reliable electricity or clean cooking fuel increasingly enjoy a degree of dignity and convenience.
Small businesses accept digital payments from customers.
Young creators from places far from India’s traditional centres of opportunity now participate in a national economy connected by roads, phones and digital networks.
The biggest change is not any individual programme.
It is that prosperity feels more widely distributed.
One senses movement.
One senses confidence.
Above all, one senses that millions more Indians now expect their children to live better lives than they did.
Of course, none of this emerged from a vacuum.
Connective tissue.
India’s progress did not begin in 2014.
It was built upon institutions, reforms and capabilities accumulated over decades.
But the defining feature of Prime Minister Modi’s era has been the game-changing acceleration, scale and execution brought to those foundations.
In earlier years, the transformation often happened incrementally and slowly.
A road here.
A bank account there.
A digital platform.
A tax reform.
An electricity connection.
A logistics corridor.
Individually, each reform seemed limited.
Under Prime Minister Modi’s leadership, they were pursued together.
Only because someone at the top insisted they be pursued together did they form the connective tissue that allowed the economy to function with greater coherence.
They created conditions for private capital to be deployed, not merely promised.
They were accompanied by stronger public institutions and public sector enterprises, not as relics of an earlier era but as instruments of national capability.

Whether securing oil supplies, acquiring critical minerals, supporting defence manufacturing, kickstarting clean energy markets or helping create new industrial ecosystems, they increasingly acted with the confidence of a country determined not merely to participate in global supply chains, but to shape them.
Brick by brick, India has been building.
Faster in some areas, slower in the others, but with a visible spine connecting the effort.
That confidence has also been tested.
Over the last decade, India has navigated a pandemic, global supply chain disruptions, energy price shocks, conflicts in Ukraine and West Asia, and a more fragmented geopolitical landscape.

Through these tests, one sensed a country increasingly confident in its capacity to act, whether by vaccinating hundreds of millions of people, evacuating citizens from conflict zones, or maintaining stability and growth amid global turbulence.
The consistency sends a powerful signal beyond India’s shores.
It tells a lender in Singapore or a pension fund in Toronto that the direction will not reverse with political cycles or global uncertainty.
Capital, which is risk-averse, grows braver in the presence of that kind of leadership.
Yet, in my view, the most consequential change may have occurred in a field that will define the coming century: Energy and climate.
Deeper transformationFor much of modern history, energy security was synonymous with access to oil and gas.
Economic growth depended on resources concentrated in distant geographies, often vulnerable to conflict and disruption.
Prime Minister Modi recognised earlier than most that the clean energy transition could offer India a different path.
I remember in 2015 when he announced India’s bold renewable energy ambitions to the world.
I was in Glasgow in 2021 when he announced India’s commitment to net zero by 2070.
Many international observers did not expect India to make such a pledge.
But the significance of those moments went far beyond the targets themselves.
They signalled a deeper transformation.
Clean energy is now meeting most of the growth in India’s electricity demand, helping power factories, irrigation pumps, Global Capability Centres and the digital economy.
India is manufacturing equipment, building transmission networks, investing in storage and developing cleaner fuels.
We are on the path to insulating ourselves from being held hostage to crises or decisions made elsewhere.

In fact, the availability of abundant clean energy is helping position India as one of the world’s most attractive destinations for data centres, advanced manufacturing and semiconductors—new-age industries creating opportunities for further prosperity.
Underlying all of this is a simple but profound idea: Clean energy is not merely climate policy.
It is economic security.
It is strategic autonomy.
It is nation building.
ReNew is, in many ways, a product of Prime Minister Modi’s larger vision.
Over fifteen years, we have grown into one of India’s largest clean energy companies, with a balance sheet of more than $11 billion and a pipeline approaching 28 GW.
We generate almost a tenth of India’s solar and wind power, have created over 100,000 jobs directly and indirectly, and have connected global capital to the Indian opportunity.
But ours is only one of many such stories.
Across sectors, entrepreneurs have built companies, industries and capabilities because a leader set the ambition, built the ground beneath it and stayed the course.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi (front R) and French President Emmanuel Macron (front L) pose with world leaders and representatives for a group picture at the start of the founding conference of the International Solar Alliance in New Delhi on March 11, 2018.

The International Solar Alliance (ISA) organizes more than 121 "sunshine" countries that are situated or have territory between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn, with the aim of boosting solar energy output in an effort to reduce global dependence on fossil fuels.
(Photo by Ludovic MARIN / AFP)A very different futureCan we provide round-the-clock clean, reliable power to every home, factory and data centre?
Can we secure critical minerals, deepen manufacturing capabilities, master artificial intelligence and create globally competitive industries in technologies that are only now emerging?
Can we ensure that every Indian enjoys cleaner air, better opportunities and a quality of life that matches the best in the world?
These questions will require patient institution building, long-term investment and relentless execution.
They will demand the same discipline that got us here.
India has been fortunate to have, in Prime Minister Modi, an architect and a visionary who understands these issues intuitively and is willing to spearhead them.
Under his leadership, India has begun to believe in its own capacity to build at the scale of its ambitions.
Once a nation acquires that belief, its future begins to look very different from its past.
This self confidence, and its manifestation in action, will be Prime Minister Modi’s most enduring contribution to India.

article_sentences: Retail investors holding the securities said they had not received coupon payments due on October 18, three days after the Supreme Court ruling.
In a letter to Axis Trustee Services Ltd, reviewed by Reuters, investors sought clarity on the payments and urged the debenture trustee to intervene.
“We call upon the Trustee to obtain immediate written confirmation from Yes Bank as to whether this coupon has been paid, cancelled, or remains outstanding,” the bondholders said in the letter.
However, the sources cited by Reuters said the bond documentation gives Yes Bank discretion over coupon payments.
The question of payment can be considered only after the AT-1 bonds are reinstated on the bank’s balance sheet.

On October 15, the Supreme Court dismissed appeals filed by Yes Bank, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Union government, upholding the Bombay High Court’s January 20, 2023, judgment against the write-off of AT-1 bonds worth ₹8,415 crore.
The write-down was carried out in March 2020 as part of Yes Bank’s reconstruction, when the lender was facing a severe financial crisis.
The ruling marks a significant legal victory for investors whose holdings were cancelled during the rescue.
The bank’s administrator had written down the bonds as part of the reconstruction process, prompting Axis Trustee Services and other bondholders to challenge the move in court.
Why were Yes Bank’s AT-1 bonds written off?
Yes Bank plunged into a liquidity crisis in March 2020 as bad loans mounted.
The RBI took control of the lender and imposed restrictions on withdrawals.

stories.headline: Former Radio Kashmir Director Bashir Arif appointed to Muslim Personal Law Board J&K
stories.title: Former Radio Kashmir Director Bashir Arif appointed to Muslim Personal Law Board J&K
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 23: Veteran broadcaster, poet and former Director of Radio Kashmir Srinagar, Bashir Arif, has been appointed as a member of the Muslim Personal Law Board Jammu and Kashmir, along with six other members. Arif, who also served as Deputy Director General of All India Radio, is a prominent figure in Kashmir's broadcasting and literary circles. He has contributed to Kashmiri radio, television, theatre and literature over several decades. According to an order issued by the Board, the appointments were made in consultation with Chairman Mufti Nasir-ul-Islam Farooqi, Vice Chairman Syed Mohammad Aslam Andrabi, General Secretary Prof M Yaseen Kirmani and the Executive Committee. Besides Arif, the newly appointed members include Mushtaq Ahmed Pandow, Molvi Abdul Lateef Wani, Mufti Mushtaq Ahmed Kambay, Mufti Umer Qasmi, Gulzar Ahmed Charloo and Syed Muzamil Rizvi. Mufti Umer Qasmi has been inducted as a youth member, while Gulzar Ahmed Charloo and Syed Muzamil Rizvi have been appointed as members representing social activism. The Board said the appointments were aimed at strengthening its organisational structure and expanding efforts to safeguard Muslim Personal Law, promote religious and social welfare and address issues concerning the Muslim community across Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh. The order was issued by Er Danish Reshi, Advisor to the Grand Mufti of Jammu and Kashmir and General Secretary (Organisation) of the Board. All seven appointments have come into effect immediately.

stories.headline: ‘Monitor geopolitics closely, remain prepared to respond to immediate challenges’: Rajnath to Army Commanders
stories.title: ‘Monitor geopolitics closely, remain prepared to respond to immediate challenges’: Rajnath to Army Commanders
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 23: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh has exhorted the Army Commanders to closely monitor geopolitical as well as regional developments and remain prepared for future challenges. Addressing the Army Commanders’ Conference in New Delhi on October 23, 2026, he emphasised the need for a long-term strategic vision spanning the next 20-30 years, and called upon the senior leadership of the Indian Army to remain equally prepared to respond to immediate and emerging challenges. He stressed that strategies must remain dynamic and flexible, enabling timely adjustments to changing circumstances. Commending the Defence Forces for adapting to evolving operational circumstances, Rajnath Singh highlighted that innovative thinking, enhanced synergy and superior coordination, complemented by advanced weaponry, contributed to the success of Operation Sindoor. The operation sent a clear message that India would not hesitate to take necessary measures to safeguard its national interests, he said. Defence Minister appreciated the military’s restructuring efforts, with a special focus on the use of drones and modern technology. He stressed the need to strengthen capabilities, continuously assess performance, and implement necessary improvements in line with evolving circumstances. He underscored the importance of accelerating efforts in areas such as artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, data analytics, cybersecurity, and secure communication networks. Rajnath Singh emphasised that despite growing significance of challenges across the air, maritime, space and cyber domains, land warfare and ground forces would remain indispensable. He called for an integrated approach to modern warfare, stressing that success would depend on multi-domain capabilities and seamless coordination in joint operations. Defence Minister acknowledged the self-reliance efforts of the defence forces, stating that India’s growing defence manufacturing capabilities are a result of concerted efforts of all stakeholders. “Amidst the changing global landscape, Prime Minister Narendra Modi-led Government is prioritising Aatmanirbharta in defence. In the financial year 2025-26, defence production surged to a record Rs 1.78 lakh crore, with defence exports reaching an all-time high of approx. Rs 38,000 crore,” he said. Referring to the ‘Year of Reforms - 2025’, Rajnath Singh stated that reform is a continuous process, the success of which depends on effective implementation. He urged the Commanders to drive these reforms forward within their respective commands and echelons, while ensuring that they translate into tangible benefits for operational capabilities. Defence Minister credited the valour, discipline, preparedness and restraint of the Defence Forces, along with the dynamic leadership and diplomatic efforts of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, for strengthening India’s global standing. He urged the Defence Forces to maintain their focus on self-reliance, effective implementation of reforms, improved manpower management, greater participation of women and an integrated approach to national security. On the occasion, Defence Minister released the Land Warfare Doctrine, which provides an overarching framework to prepare the Indian Army to meet the challenges posed by the evolving character of warfare and future conflicts. He also unveiled the annual United Nations Journal and felicitated Indian Army personnel who have made notable contributions while serving as United Nations peacekeepers, recognising their exemplary service, professionalism and contribution to international peace and security. MoS Defence Sanjay Seth, Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani, Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth, Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh and other senior officials were present on the occasion. With its comprehensive agenda, the conference has been organised to provide an important forum for the senior leadership of the Indian Army to review ongoing initiatives, identify future thrust areas and formulate appropriate policy directions towards building a progressive, adaptive, technologically enabled and future-ready Indian Army.

stories.headline: UDF-led Keralam govt sanctions Vigilance probe against CPI(M) leader P.P. Divya over alleged tender irregularities
stories.title: UDF-led Keralam govt sanctions Vigilance probe against CPI(M) leader P.P. Divya over alleged tender irregularities
stories.summary: Officials say Home Minister Ramesh Chennithala sanctioned inquiry into award of ₹12-crore contract to private firm to construct modular toilets allegedly without inviting open tenders and thereby bypassing competitive bidding
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Keralam government on Friday ordered an anti-corruption investigation against former Kannur district panchayat president and Communist Party of India (Marxist) [CPI(M)] leader P.P. Divya.

Officials said Home Minister Ramesh Chennithala sanctioned the inquiry into the award of a ₹12-crore contract to a private firm to construct modular toilets, allegedly without inviting open tenders and thereby bypassing competitive bidding.
By sanctioning the probe, under Section 17 (A) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, Mr Chennithala opened the door to the Vigilance investigation.
According to Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau (VACB) officials, government sanction does not preclude a preliminary inquiry or require the outright registration of an FIR.

They noted that, in earlier cases, the VACB had conducted a preliminary inquiry to determine whether the allegations disclosed a cognisable offence under the Prevention of Corruption (PC) Act before registering an FIR.
They said the Supreme Court, in several orders, had reiterated the need for a preliminary inquiry before registering a Vigilance offence against those who held public office.
However, officials said registering an FIR by the VACB would automatically trigger an Enforcement Directorate (ED) investigation under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA).

Earlier, the Kerala Students Union (KSU) vice president had moved the government, alleging that Ms Divya and her husband, V.P. Ajith, had links with the firm and the company was a front for the CPI(M) leader.
Both Ms Divya and Mr Ajith denied the accusation and said the complaint was politically motivated.

The CPI(M) had removed Ms Divya from the post of Kannur district president after the police booked her on the charge of abetting the death by suicide of former Kannur Additional District Magistrate Naveen Babu.

Naveen Babu’s death, following an allegedly defamatory speech by Ms Divya at his farewell function at the Kannur District Collectorate, put the CPI(M) on the defensive in Kannur and his home district of Pathanamthitta.

The Communist Party of India (CPI), which held the Revenue portfolio in the previous Left Democratic Front (LDF) dispensation, demanded Ms Divya’s prosecution and cautioned the CPI(M) against giving her any political protection.

body: By sanctioning the probe, under Section 17 (A) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, Mr Chennithala opened the door to the Vigilance investigation.
According to Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau (VACB) officials, government sanction does not preclude a preliminary inquiry or require the outright registration of an FIR.

They noted that, in earlier cases, the VACB had conducted a preliminary inquiry to determine whether the allegations disclosed a cognisable offence under the Prevention of Corruption (PC) Act before registering an FIR.
They said the Supreme Court, in several orders, had reiterated the need for a preliminary inquiry before registering a Vigilance offence against those who held public office.
However, officials said registering an FIR by the VACB would automatically trigger an Enforcement Directorate (ED) investigation under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA).

Earlier, the Kerala Students Union (KSU) vice president had moved the government, alleging that Ms Divya and her husband, V.P. Ajith, had links with the firm and the company was a front for the CPI(M) leader.
Both Ms Divya and Mr Ajith denied the accusation and said the complaint was politically motivated.

The CPI(M) had removed Ms Divya from the post of Kannur district president after the police booked her on the charge of abetting the death by suicide of former Kannur Additional District Magistrate Naveen Babu.
